events.summary: Solid first cut, well-supported by UF/IFAS (EDIS ST106/ENH265), Kew POWO, World Flora Online, and Richard Lyons Nursery. Confidence is high on range, morphology, bark, and Florida landscape performance. Butterfly/pollinator specifics and wood-dust safety are the weakest fields — no authoritative lepidopteran host record found, and wood-dust irritation applies only to woodworkers, not park visitors.

events.feedback:
CRITICAL BOTANICAL & DATABASE CORRECTIONS

Index Flag Mismatch (Nectar Flag): Current Index Flag is Nectar - no. Text Conflict: Under Wildlife Value, the profile explicitly states "The yellow summer flowers draw bees and other generalist pollinators, and butterflies visiting for nectar are a regular sight when the tree is in bloom." Alignment: Toggle Nectar to yes so database search filters match the prose.

DEEPENING BOTANICAL & ECOLOGICAL NUANCE

Exfoliating Bark Morphology: The draft notes that "smooth bark peels away in thin strips to reveal a mottled surface." Botanical Detail: Elevate this morphological description by identifying the process as exfoliating rhytidome shedding in thin papery squamules/strips, exposing the green, photosynthetic outer phelloderm (cortex) underneath.

Taxonomic Revision Context: The text mentions taxonomic shuffling between Caesalpinia and Libidibia. Botanical Detail: Note that Libidibia punctata was resurrected and transferred out of Caesalpinia sens

events.feedback:
Final Minor Polish Opportunities
Local Phenology: Consider explicitly noting the late spring/early summer flush so park patrons know when to expect the primary flowering window in Manatee County.

Flower Morphology Detail: In the REPRODUCTION block, mentioning the slightly zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetrical) flowers characteristic of Caesalpinioideae would add one more subtle touch for visiting botanists.

This entry is authoritative, highly readable, and thoroughly researched. It easily sets the standard for public botanical documentation.
